events.description: General anaesthesia induction, intubation, CO2 pneumoperitoneum 12 mmHg and Trendelenburg positioning

evidence.quote: The patient was induced with intravenous fentanyl (2 µg kg^(-1)), propofol (3 mg kg^(-1)), and rocuronium (0.6 mg kg^(-1)). Direct endotracheal intubation was atraumatic, and the patient was maintained under general anaesthesia with sevoflurane. The patient’s abdomen was insufflated with CO_(2 )gas to 12 mmHg, was placed in Trendelenburg position, and the surgery progressed uneventfully.

events.description: First desaturation with clinical examination (ETT in position, clear lungs)

evidence.quote: Twenty minutes into the case, the SpO_(2) suddenly dropped from 99% to 94%. Vitals were BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, EtCO_(2) 35 mmHg, and Ppeak 22 cmH_(2)O. On a clinical exam, the endotracheal tube remained in appropriate position, lung sounds were clear without rales, and the SpO_(2) remained between 94% and 96%.

events.description: Further desaturation to 84% with normal airway pressure and tidal volume

evidence.quote: However, after 5 minutes, the SpO_(2) dropped to 84%, and the EtCO_(2) decreased to 32 mmHg with a BP of 120/70 mmHg. Airway pressures remained normal: (Ppeak 22 cmH_(2)O), and a expiratory tidal volume (VTe) of 7 mL kg^(-1) was maintained.

events.description: Desufflation, supine repositioning, ventilator check, suctioning and manual ventilation with recovery

evidence.quote: The surgery team was notified; the abdomen was desufflated and the patient was repositioned to the zero degree supine position. The ventilator was checked, minimal sputum was aspirated from the endotracheal tube, and the patient was ventilated manually with an ambu bag. After 5 minutes, SpO_(2) improved to 97% and BP improved to 115/70 mmHg.

events.description: Intraoperative differential reasoning (normal airway pressure, correct tube, minimal blood loss) and first suspicion of PE before open conversion

evidence.quote: Potential causes for these changes could include bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, pneumothorax, cardiogenic shock, hypovolemic shock, or obstructive shock. However, the patient exhibited no evidence of elevated airway pressures; the endotracheal tube was correctly positioned, VTe was adequate, and there was minimal blood loss during surgery. Given the identified patient risk factors, we raised suspicion for PE. Since open hysterectomy has less respiratory and hemodynamic effects compared to laparoscopy, the decision was made to convert to an open procedure after multidisciplinary discussion. According to the European Society of Cardiology guidelines, bedside echocardiography and if feasible, CTPA, should be performed promptly when PE is suspected in a patient with hemodynamic instability. In this case, the patient, with a ten-year history of hypertension, was suspected of having hemodynamically unstable PE due to hypotension requiring vasopressor support, despite ruling out iatrogenic causes, hemorrhagic and distributive shock. Following the procedure, a CTPA, D-dimer, transthoracic echocardiography, assessment of right ventricular function, and ABG analysis were obtained to establish an early diagnosis of PE and guide management.

events.description: Laparoscopy resumed; re-insufflation desaturation, EtCO2 fall and hypotension
events.time_text: upon abdominal insufflation and positioning the patient in Trendelenburg

evidence.quote: At this point, it was decided to resume the procedure laparoscopically. However, upon abdominal insufflation and positioning the patient in Trendelenburg, the SpO_(2) dropped rapidly to 89-90%, EtCO_(2) decreased from 38 mmHg to 30 mmHg, and BP dropped to 95/50 mmHg.

events.description: Conversion to open surgery with stabilised vitals and completion of the hysterectomy

evidence.quote: Due to the hemodynamic changes with insufflation, the surgical team decided to convert to open surgery. Following abdominal desufflation and opening of the abdomen, the patient’s vitals remained stable with an SpO_(2) of 97-98%, HR of 86-95 bpm, BP of 110/80-130/80 mmHg, and EtCO_(2) of 32-35 mmHg.

events.description: Extubation after procedure completion

evidence.quote: The patient was extubated without difficulty when the procedure was completed 1 hour later.

events.description: Post-extubation hypoxemia, supplemental oxygen and transfer to recovery room

evidence.quote: However, shortly after extubation, the SpO_(2) decreased to 90-92% on room air, and an arterial blood gas (ABG) was indicated. Supplemental O_(2) was administered via nasal cannula at 5 L min^(-1) and she was transferred to the recovery room with SpO_(2) 94% and BP 105/60 mmHg

events.description: Suspicion of PE and bedside work-up: echocardiogram, ECG, chest X-ray, laboratory tests and ABG

evidence.quote: After excluding possible surgical causes, we had a high suspicion of PE due to air or thrombi, with an simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index score of 3 points. A transthoracic echocardiogram was performed showing right heart dilatation, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 60 mmHg (Figure 1). The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and S1Q3 sign (Figure 2). A chest X-ray showed evidence of cardiomegaly (Figure 3). The remarkable laboratory tests showed elevated D-dimer 4213 ng mL^(-1), lactate 2.1 mmol L^(-1), hs-troponin T 0.021 ng mL^(-1), Pro BNP 1601 pg mL^(-1), and ABG results with pH 7.36, PaO_(2) 90 mmHg, PaCO_(2) 35 mmHg. Acute PE was strongly suspected.

events.description: CTPA confirming acute PE with pulmonary hypertension findings

evidence.quote: A CTPA was obtained to confirm the presence of a PE (Figure 4), which also showed evidence of pulmonary hypertension (Figure 5).

events.description: Multidisciplinary consultation confirms acute PE secondary to DVT and heparin is started

evidence.quote: Multidisciplinary consultations, including cardiology, interventional radiology, obstetrics and gynecology, cardiothoracic surgery, and critical care, confirmed acute PE secondary to deep vein thrombosis. The patient was treated with intravenous heparin bolus 5000 IU followed by a 500 IU/hour infusion.

events.description: ICU admission with hemodynamic monitoring and noradrenaline infusion up to 24 hours

evidence.quote: The patient was admitted to the ICU presenting with mild hypoxemia, HR 115 bpm, BP 95/60 mmHg no altered mental status, and no shock symptoms.
The patient was admitted to the ICU for hemodynamic monitoring requiring a noradrenaline infusion up to 0.1 mcg kg^(-1) min^(-1) for 24 hours.

events.description: Systemic thrombolysis judged contraindicated by moderate postoperative bleeding risk

evidence.quote: Post-hysterectomy, the risk of postoperative bleeding was classified as moderate, placing her in a group contraindicated for systemic thrombolytic therapy.

events.description: Planned contingency only: intravascular thrombectomy with IVC filter if hemodynamic instability occurred; no thrombectomy documented

evidence.quote: If hemodynamic instability occurred, intravascular thrombectomy and placement of an IVC filter in the catheterization lab would be considered.

events.description: Lower-extremity DVT ultrasound and CT venography: left popliteal and right common iliac DVT

evidence.quote: Deep venous thrombosis ultrasound and CT venography of the lower extremities were performed, showing the left popliteal vein and acute thrombosis localized to the right common iliac vein, respectively.

events.description: IVC filter inserted transjugularly by interventional radiology

evidence.quote: An inferior vena cava filter was subsequently inserted by interventional radiology via a transjugular approach (Figure 6).

events.description: POD 3: heparin infusion stopped and oral rivaroxaban started

evidence.quote: On POD 3, the heparin infusion was discontinued, and the patient was transitioned to oral rivaroxaban, 30 mg day^(-1).

events.description: POD 5: discharged from ICU

evidence.quote: The patient was discharged from the ICU on POD 5.

summary.text: A 51-year-old woman (BMI 26 kg m^(2-1) as printed) with hypertension (ten-year history) and newly diagnosed type II diabetes had menorrhagia from uterine adenomyosis. She had been taking prescribed oral Desogestrel and tranexamic acid and self-prescribed Panax notoginseng, described as 3 months prior to the operation. Because medical management failed, a laparoscopic total hysterectomy under general anaesthesia was scheduled; preoperative echocardiogram (LVEF 72%), chest X-ray, airway/cardiopulmonary examination and baseline vitals were normal.

After induction, intubation, CO2 pneumoperitoneum (12 mmHg) and Trendelenburg positioning, SpO2 fell 20 minutes into the case (99% to 94%) and then to 84% with EtCO2 32 mmHg despite correct tube position, clear lungs and normal airway pressure. Desufflation, supine positioning and manual ventilation improved SpO2 to 97%; with minimal blood loss and no airway explanation, PE was suspected intraoperatively. When laparoscopy was resumed, SpO2 fell to 89-90%, EtCO2 fell from 38 to 30 mmHg and BP fell to 95/50 mmHg, and surgery was converted to open with stable vitals; the procedure was completed and she was extubated.

Shortly after extubation SpO2 was 90-92% on room air, treated with nasal oxygen 5 L/min; she went to the recovery room (SpO2 94%, BP 105/60). After excluding surgical causes, PE was strongly suspected (provisional) with sPESI 3; echocardiography showed right heart dilatation/strain, mild TR and PASP 60 mmHg, ECG sinus rhythm with S1Q3, chest X-ray cardiomegaly, D-dimer 4213 ng/mL, lactate 2.1 mmol/L, hs-troponin T 0.021 ng/mL, Pro BNP 1601 pg/mL and ABG pH 7.36, PaO2 90, PaCO2 35 mmHg. CTPA confirmed acute PE with findings suggesting pulmonary hypertension; ultrasound and CT venography showed left popliteal and right common iliac DVT.

The authors suspected hemodynamically unstable PE (hypotension requiring vasopressor support, after ruling out iatrogenic, hemorrhagic and distributive causes), but on ICU admission she had mild hypoxemia, HR 115, BP 95/60, no altered mental status and no shock symptoms. Moderate postoperative bleeding risk made systemic thrombolysis contraindicated. She received intravenous unfractionated heparin (5000 IU bolus, 500 IU/hour), ICU hemodynamic monitoring and noradrenaline up to 0.1 mcg/kg/min for 24 hours, and an IVC filter was inserted transjugularly. Thrombectomy was only a contingency if instability occurred; none is documented as performed. Heparin was stopped and oral rivaroxaban 30 mg/day started on POD 3; she was discharged from the ICU on POD 5 (no later outcome reported).
